title: OCULAR & ORBITAL TRAUMA: COMPLETE CLINICAL PROTOCOL
summary: An exhaustive guide to the diagnosis, management, and surgical repair of periocular, orbital, and globe injuries. This protocol prioritizes visual preservation and structural integrity through meticulous examination and evidence-based interventions.

sections.title: EYELID TRAUMA: PERIOCULAR HAEMATOMA
content: Definition: A ‘black eye’ consists of a haematoma (focal collection of blood) and/or periocular ecchymosis (diffuse bruising) and oedema (Fig. 22.1A).
Most common blunt injury to the eyelid or forehead; generally innocuous.
Critical Exclusion 1: Trauma to the globe or orbit. Examine before oedema sets in. Use gentle sustained pressure to open lids; never apply force to the globe.
Critical Exclusion 2: Orbital roof fracture. Suspect if associated with subconjunctival haemorrhage without a visible posterior limit (Fig. 22.1B).
Critical Exclusion 3: Basal skull fracture. Characterized by bilateral ring haematomas (‘panda eyes’ – Fig. 22.1C).
Imaging: Consider CT, MRI, or bedside ultrasonography (with meticulous care) if clinical visualization is impossible.

sections.title: LID LACERATIONS: MANAGEMENT & REPAIR
sections.content: The presence of a lid laceration, however insignificant, mandates careful exploration of the wound and examination of the globe and adnexal structures. Any lid defect should be repaired by direct closure whenever possible, even under tension, since this affords the best functional and cosmetic result (Fig. 22.2A and B). Superficial lacerations parallel to the lid margin without gaping can be sutured with 6-0 black silk or nylon; sutures removed after 5–6 days. Infection is always a risk, even from a small laceration (Fig. 22.2C). Lacerations with mild tissue loss just sufficient to prevent direct primary closure can usually be managed by performing a lateral cantholysis. Extensive tissue loss may require major reconstructive procedures similar to malignant tumour resection.

sections.title: STEP-BY-STEP: LID MARGIN SUTURING
content: Step 1: Vertical Mattress Suture. Insert a 5-0 silk suture in line with meibomian gland orifices, 2 mm from edges and 2 mm deep; leave untied.
Step 2: Tarsal Plate Alignment. Bring edges together with partial-thickness lamellar 5-0 absorbable (e.g., polyglactin) sutures tied anteriorly.
Step 3: Tie Margin Suture. Tie the 5-0 silk so cut edges slightly pucker; leave ends long (~2 cm).
Step 4: Skin Closure. Use interrupted 6-0 or 7-0 nylon or absorbable sutures.
Step 5: Knot Security. Secure the silk suture ends to direct them and knots away from the cornea.

sections.title: CANALICULAR & AUXILIARY MANAGEMENT
content: Canalicular Lacerations: Repair within 24 hours (Fig. 22.3A).
Bridging: Use silicone tubing (Crawford tube) tied in the nose or a monocanalicular stent (Mini Monoka – Fig. 22.3B).
Fixation: Suture footplate to lid with 8-0 material; leave tubing in situ for 3–6 months.
Tetanus Status: Satisfactory status is mandatory. No prior immunization: 250 units human tetanus immunoglobulin (IM). Previously immunized (>10 years): subcutaneous tetanus toxoid booster.
Foreign Bodies: CT scan required for any suspicion in soft tissues or orbit (Fig. 22.4A-D).

sections.title: CRITICAL TRAUMA WARNINGS
content: Bilateral ‘panda’ eyes = Possible skull-base fracture.
Orbital cellulitis risk exists for any penetrating lid laceration, especially with retained foreign bodies.
NEVER apply force on the globe until integrity is confirmed.
Low IOP with a full hyphaema = Suspect occult posterior scleral rupture.
NO MRI if a ferrous metallic foreign body is suspected.
Avoid nose blowing in orbital floor/medial wall fractures.

branches: Mechanism: Sudden pressure increase from object >5cm (fist/tennis ball)
Signs: Ecchymosis, oedema, subcutaneous emphysema, infraorbital nerve anaesthesia
Diplopia: From haemorrhage/oedema (tightening septa) or mechanical entrapment (Inf. Rectus/Oblique)
Enophthalmos: Manifests after days; 20% have >2mm at 6 months
Diagnosis: Visual acuity, CT (coronal sections), Hess Chart, Forced Duction Test
Treatment: Observation, antibiotics, ice, nasal decongestants, steroids for nerve compromise
Surgery: Required within 2 weeks for persistent diplopia, >50% floor involvement, or enophthalmos >2mm

content.explanation: Typically seen in patients <18 years due to bone elasticity. Minimal external signs but acute tissue incarceration. Symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, headache, persistent oculocardiac reflex. Requires URGENT repair to avoid permanent damage.

rows: Common in children (sharp object/minor blow). Adults (major trauma). Signs: Upper lid haematoma, CSF leak risk (meningitis), globe pulsation.
Usually associated with floor fractures. Signs: Subcutaneous emphysema (on nose blowing), defective abduction/adduction (medial rectus entrapment).
Rare. Solid bone; usually associated with extensive facial damage.

sections.title: ORBITAL (RETROBULBAR) HAEMORRHAGE
content: Risk: Acute orbital compartment syndrome and irreversible blindness.
Signs: Proptosis, haemorrhagic chemosis, high IOP, APD, optic disc swelling.
Canthotomy: 1-2 cm horizontal full-thickness incision at lateral canthus angle under local anaesthesia.
Cantholysis: Retract lower lid, cut inferior crus of lateral canthal tendon directed inferiorly/parallel to rim.
Extension: If necessary, cut superior limb of tendon (caution: adnexal damage risk).

rows: Full-thickness wound where globe gives way at weakest point.
Single full-thickness wound; no exit wound.

sections.title: IMAGING MODALITIES IN GLOBE TRAUMA
content: Plain Radiographs: Detect foreign bodies; metallic ones move during upgaze/downgaze.
Ultrasonography: Useful for IOFBs, globe rupture, retinal detachment. Use gentle technique.
CT Scan: Superior for detecting and localizing IOFBs (Fig. 22.11B-D) and evaluating bony structures.
MRI: Superior for injuries of the globe (e.g., occult posterior rupture) but contraindicated for ferrous IOFBs.
Electrodiagnostics: Assess optic nerve and retinal integrity, especially with retained IOFB.

branches: Cornea: Abrasion (fluorescein stain), Acute oedema, Descemet tears (vertical/birth trauma)
Hyphaema: Blood in AC settling inferiorly. High IOP risk leads to ischaemic optic neuropathy/blood staining
Iris: Vossius ring (pigment on lens), Traumatic mydriasis, radial tears, Iridodialysis (D-shaped)
Lens: Rosette cataract, Subluxation (iridodonesis), Dislocation (into vitreous or AC)
IOP: Angle recession (6-9% late glaucoma risk), Hypotony (suspect occult injury)
Globe Rupture: Usually anterior at Schlemm canal; prolapse of iris/lens/vitreous

sections.title: BLUNT TRAUMA: POSTERIOR COMPLICATIONS
content: Vitreous Haemorrhage: Often associated with PVD and 'tobacco dust' (pigment cells).
Commotio Retinae: Concussion-induced cloudy swelling (grey appearance). Temporal fundus typical. 'Cherry-red spot' if macula involved. Resolves in ~6 weeks.
Chorioretinitis Sclopetaria: High-velocity projectile splits chorioretinal layers exposing intact sclera. 15% achieve 6/6 vision.
Choroidal Rupture: Involves Bruch membrane/RPE. Fresh rupture obscured by blood; old rupture appears as white crescentic streak. Late CNVM risk.
Retinal Dialysis: Break at ora serrata from traction. Most common superonasal/inferotemporal. Can lead to slow-progressing RD.
Macular Hole: Occurs at time of injury or after commotio resolution.
Choroidal Detachment: Occurs in soft eyes; must distinguish from RD.

sections.title: TRAUMATIC OPTIC NEUROPATHY (TON)
sections.content: Occurs in up to 5% of facial fractures. Classification: Direct (bone fragments/projectile) or Indirect (force transmission, shearing, vasospasm). Presentation: Sudden visual loss (50% light perception only), APD, initially normal fundus with pallor developing over weeks. Management: Individualized imaging (CT for bone, MRI for soft tissue). Treatment: Spontaneous improvement in ~50% of indirect cases. Steroids (IV methylprednisolone) within 8 hours remain controversial (CRASH study notes death risk in brain injury). Decompression considered for visual decline despite steroids or bony compression. Optic Nerve Avulsion: Striking cavity where nerve head retracted; no treatment.

sections.title: ABUSIVE HEAD TRAUMA (SHAKEN BABY)
content: Demographics: Children < 2 years. Mortality > 25%; responsible for 50% of child abuse deaths.
Mechanism: Rotational acceleration/deceleration. Hypoxia, raised ICP, and ischaemia.
Systemic Signs: Irritability, lethargy, vomiting, skull/rib/long bone fractures, subdural haemorrhage.
Ocular Features: Retinal haemorrhages (80% bilateral) involving multiple layers from posterior pole to periphery. APD, poor visual response.
Visual Outcome: Visual loss in 20% (largely from cerebral damage).

sections.title: PENETRATING TRAUMA PROTOCOLS
sections.content: Penetrating injuries are 3x more common in males (50% aged 15–34). High risk of endophthalmitis/panophthalmitis. Prophylactic intravitreal antibiotics (vancomycin) recommended. Ascertain tetanus status. Most need URGENT surgical repair under general anaesthesia. TECHNIQUE: Small corneal wounds may heal with bandage contact lens. Medium wounds: 10-0 nylon (shorter stitches near visual axis). Iris involvement: Reposition if possible; excise if necrotic/contaminated. Lens damage: Suturing followed by phacoemulsification/vitrectomy. Scleral: Anterior wounds have better prognosis than posterior. Use 8-0 nylon or 7-0 polyglactin. Reposit viable uveal tissue; cut prolapsed vitreous flush.

sections.title: TRAUMATIC RETINAL DETACHMENT (RD)
content: Trauma accounts for ~10% of all RD cases; most common cause in children.
Mechanism: Vitreous incarceration in penetrating wounds leads to fibroblastic proliferation.
Progression: Contraction of epiretinal fibrosis causes anterior tractional RD.
Delayed Risk: Retinal breaks may develop weeks later, leading to rapid rhegmatogenous RD.
Prognosis Factors: Initial VA, APD, IOFB presence, infection, and extent of retinal injury.
